'''Marvin Philip Kahl''' (September 28, 1934 – December 4, 2012) was an American [[zoologist]] who studied [[birds]] and [[elephants]]. From the 1950s to 1980s, Kahl conducted his avian research on [[storks]], [[flamingos]] and [[spoonbills]]. During this time period, Kahl worked for various places including the [[National Audubon Society]] and [[Rare Animal Relief Effort]]. In the 1990s, Kahl switched his research to elephants and continued to study them until the 2010s.

Throughout his career, Kahl took wildlife photographs for various publications including ''[[National Geographic]]'' and the ''[[Journal of Zoology]].'' Kahl wrote ''Wonders of Storks'' in 1978 and was a co-author of ''Storks, Ibises, and Spoonbills of the World'' in 1992. Apart from his works, Kahl received a fellowship from the [[National Science Foundation]] in the 1960s and one from the [[American Museum of Natural History]] in the 1970s. He also became part of the [[MacArthur Fellows Program]] in 1988.

==Early life and education==
Kahl was born in [[Indianapolis, Indiana]], on September 28, 1934.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=KAHL, M(arvin) P(hilip) 1934–|date=1983|encyclopedia=Contemporary Authors|publisher=Gale Research Company|location=Detroit|url=https://archive.org/details/contemporaryauth107halm/page/236/mode/2up|access-date=January 19, 2021|editor-last=May|editor-first=Hal|volume=107|page=237|isbn=0810319071}}</ref> Growing up, Kahl enjoyed learning about nature when he was a child and began [[birdwatching]] while in high school.<ref name=Harris1964>{{cite news |last1=Harris |first1=Punch |title=Stork Took Her Son To Africa, Says Mother Of Ornithologist |work=The Indianapolis Star |date=June 21, 1964 |at=sec. 5 p. 2}}</ref> For his post-secondary education, Kahl studied botany and zoology at [[Butler University]] and received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in 1956.<ref name=IndianapolisStar1995>{{cite news |title=M. Philip Kahl |work=The Indianapolis Star |date=April 25, 1995 |page=F8}}</ref><ref name=Commire1985>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=KAHL, M(arvin) P(hilip) 1934–|date=1985|encyclopedia=Something About The Author|publisher=Gale Research Company|location=Detroit|url=https://archive.org/details/somethingaboutau37anne/page/82/mode/2up|access-date=January 19, 2021|editor-last=Commire|editor-first=Anne|volume=37|page=82|isbn=0810300699}}</ref> After Butler, Kahl went to [[Emory University]] for a biology program while serving for the [[United States Army]].<ref name=IndianapolisStar1995/><ref name=Harris1964/> As part of the Army, he conducted research on how [[radioactivity]] impacted nature in [[Oak Ridge, Tennessee]], and [[Puerto Rico]].<ref name=Harris1964/> While studying psychology and zoology at the [[University of Georgia]], Kahl received a [[Master of Science]] and [[Doctor of Philosophy]] during the 1960s.<ref name=IndianapolisStar1995/><ref name=Americanscience>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=Kahl, Marvin Philip|date=1976|encyclopedia=American men and women of science H-K|editor=Jaques Cattell Press|publisher=R.R. Bowker Company|location=New York & London|url=https://archive.org/details/13thamericanmenw03jaqu/page/2216/mode/2up|access-date=January 19, 2021|edition=13th|volume=3|page=2216|isbn=0835208680}}</ref>

==Career==
In 1959, Kahl started a five-year position working for the [[National Audubon Society]] as a biologist.<ref name=Commire1985/> While with the NAS, Kahl conducted research on [[wood storks]] in the [[Corkscrew Swamp Sanctuary]].<ref name=Naples1970>{{cite news |title='Coming Out Party' For Storks At Audubon's Meeting |work=Naples Daily News |date=December 2, 1970 |page=38}}</ref> During the remainder of the 1960s, Kahl worked for the [[Makerere University College]] in [[Uganda]] for two years before continuing his avian research outside of the college.<ref name=Americanscience/> During this time period, Kahl studied [[storks]] with a fellowship from the [[National Science Foundation]] and a grant from ''[[National Geographic]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Shelton |first1=Sue |title=Pennies from Heaven |work=Arizona Daily Sun |date=August 10, 1988 |pages=A1–A2}}</ref>

After expanding his research to [[flamingos]] in 1964, Kahl completed his global research of every type of stork by 1970.<ref name=Hill2014p78384>{{cite journal |last1=Hill |first1=David O. |title=M. Philip Kahl, 1934–2012 |journal=The Auk |date=October 2014 |volume=131 |issue=4 |pages=783–84 |doi=10.1642/AUK-14-178.1 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=Naples1970/> During the early 1970s, Kahl worked for the [[American Museum of Natural History]] as a fellow before continuing his flamingo studies with an additional grant from ''National Geographic'' in 1972.<ref name=Commire1985/> From 1974 to 1977, Kahl was a member of the [[Rare Animal Relief Effort]] as a researcher.<ref>May ed. 1983, p. 238</ref> While branching out to research on [[spoonbills]] in 1979, Kahl finished his worldwide research on every type of flamingo in 1980.<ref name=Hill2014p78384/>

From 1980 to 1989, Kahl traveled across the world to research every spoonbill breed.<ref name=Hill2014p784>Hill 2014, p. 784</ref> During this time period, Kahl was named into the [[MacArthur Fellows Program]] in 1988.<ref>{{cite web |title=Marvin Philip Kahl |url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/338/ |website=MacArthur Foundation |access-date=20 November 2020}}</ref> With his MacArthur prize money, Kahl wanted to conduct research on the [[black-faced spoonbill]] in [[North Korea]].<ref name=Goodman1988>{{cite news |last1=Goodman |first1=Stephanie |title=Scientist feathers his nest |work=The Indianapolis Star |date=September 11, 1988 |page=H-1}}</ref> After he was not allowed to enter the country, Kahl went to [[China]] to continue his spoonbill research.<ref name=Hill2014p784/>

At the start of the 1990s, Kahl switched his research topic from birds to the non-verbal behavior of [[elephants]].<ref name=IndianapolisStar1995/> With a focus on [[African elephants]], Kahl went to [[Zimbabwe]] and conducted research at [[Hwange National Park]] throughout the 1990s. After completing his primary research, Kahl continued to review his findings until the 2010s.<ref name=Hill785>Hill 2014, p. 785</ref> Apart from his research, Kahl wrote and took photographs about wildlife for various publications including the ''[[Journal of Zoology]]'', ''National Geographic'' and ''[[Behaviour (journal)|Behaviour]]''.<ref>Shelton 1988, p. A1</ref><ref name=Goodman1988/> Some birds that Kahl photographed included the [[Salvadori's teal]] and the [[sunbittern]].<ref name=Hill2014p784/>

==Research and publications==
After raising wood storks during the early 1960s, Kahl published ''Bioenergetics of Growth in Nestlings Wood Storks'' in 1962.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kahl, Jr. |first1=M. Philip |title=Bioenergetics of Growth in Nestling Wood Storks |journal=The Condor |date=May–June 1962 |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=169–170 |doi=10.2307/1365200 |jstor=1365200}}</ref> In 1963, Kahl published his research of how storks lowered their body temperature with [[urohidrosis]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kahl Jr. |first1=M Philip |title=Thermoregulation in the Wood Stork, with Special Reference to the Role of the Legs |journal=Physiological Zoology |date=April 1963 |volume=36 |issue=2 |pages=141, 150 |doi=10.1086/physzool.36.2.30155437 |jstor=30155437}}</ref> That year, Kahl conducted an experiment with L. J. Peacock to determine how storks catch fish.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=Portrait of a Predator|date=August 23, 1963|magazine=Time Magazine|page=54|issue=8|volume=82 |issn=0040-781X}}</ref> To conduct the test, the researchers covered a wood stork's eyes with ping-pong balls that were darkened to reduce the bird's vision. After their research was concluded, Kahl and Peacock published their findings about the independent workings of the bird's feeding and sight.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kahl |first1=M. P. |last2=Peacock |first2=L. J. |title=The Bill-snap Reflex : a Feeding Mechanism in the American Wood Stork |journal=Nature |date=August 3, 1963 |volume=199 |issue=4892 |pages=505–506 |doi=10.1038/199505a0 |pmid=14058622|bibcode=1963Natur.199..505K }}</ref> As an author, Kahl wrote and drew a 1978 children's book titled ''Wonders of Storks''.<ref>Commire, ed. 1985 p. 84.</ref> As a co-writer, he was part of the 1992 publication of ''Storks, Ibises, and Spoonbills of the World''.<ref name=Hill785/>

==Death and personal life==
Kahl died from a [[brain tumor]] on December 4, 2012, in [[Sedona, Arizona]]. He was married twice and had two children.<ref>Hill 2014, pp. 782, 785</ref>
